title: AWS EBS Re-Mirroring Storm and Stuck Volumes in US-East-1

location.az: single affected Availability Zone (of the US East Region)

severity.usersAffected: Not disclosed as a user count; blast radius covered one AZ directly plus region-wide EBS/EC2/RDS control-plane degradation. Consumer sites knocked offline included Reddit, Quora, Foursquare, Hootsuite and Heroku (also Engine Yard), per CNN Money and GovTech.
severity.impactUsd: Not disclosed by AWS. Direct remedy was a 10-day service credit equal to 100% of affected customers' EBS, EC2 and RDS usage in the affected AZ; aggregate dollar figure never published.
severity.tier: Major multi-day regional service disruption (single AZ hard-down, region-wide control-plane impact)

brief: A routine network-capacity upgrade in one US-East-1 Availability Zone was executed incorrectly, shifting EBS traffic onto a low-capacity redundant network and isolating a large block of storage nodes. When connectivity returned, the nodes launched a self-reinforcing "re-mirroring storm" that exhausted spare capacity, left ~13% of the zone's volumes "stuck", and starved the region-wide EBS control plane — degrading EC2 and RDS for nearly four days and permanently losing 0.07% of the affected zone's volumes.

magnitude.note: Duration (7): ~35.7 h from the stuck volumes (00:47 PDT 21 Apr) to 97.8 % of affected-AZ volumes restored (12:30 PDT 22 Apr); the tail to the weekend of Apr 24 (~90 h from the trigger) covered the last 2.2 % of volumes and RDS. AWS's own post-mortem states RDS databases 'recovered throughout the weekend' without a precise closing time; third-party summaries cite ~7:30 PM PDT Apr 24. Blast radius: one AZ hard-down with region-wide EBS control-plane thread starvation touching all AZs; peak stuck-volume spillover to healthy zones stayed <0.07%. Financial mid: real remedy was a 10-day 100% EBS/EC2/RDS credit in the affected AZ but AWS never published a dollar total.

sequenceOfEvents.event: During a planned network-capacity upgrade in one US-East-1 AZ, engineers shifted traffic off a primary EBS router; instead of moving it to another router in the primary high-capacity network, the change routed it onto the lower-capacity redundant EBS network, which could not carry the load.
Because the redundant network also became overwhelmed/isolated, affected EBS nodes lost BOTH their primary and secondary network paths at once, cutting them off from their replica peers.

The incorrect traffic shift was rolled back; reconnected nodes immediately began searching the cluster for free space to re-establish lost data replicas, all at once. This concurrent scramble became a self-reinforcing 're-mirroring storm'.
Free capacity in the affected cluster was rapidly exhausted; nodes that could not find space entered a retry loop. About 13% of the volumes in the affected AZ became 'stuck' searching for storage.

The flood of Create Volume / re-mirror API calls caused thread starvation in the EBS control plane. Because the control plane spans the whole region, elevated error rates and latencies appeared across ALL Availability Zones, not just the failed one.

Consumer-facing sites hosted on EC2 in the region went down or degraded, including Reddit, Quora, Foursquare, Hootsuite and Heroku (also Engine Yard); the outage was public and widely reported. Press reports place the onset just before 5 a.m. ET, i.e. roughly 2 a.m. PDT.
AWS disabled all Create Volume API requests in the affected AZ to relieve the control-plane thread starvation.
With Create Volume calls blocked, EBS control-plane latencies and error rates for all other EBS-related APIs in the OTHER (healthy) Availability Zones recovered to normal.

A second wave hit: a low-probability race condition caused EBS nodes to fail when concurrently closing large numbers of replication requests, and failed re-mirror retries generated heavy control-plane negotiation, pushing an ADDITIONAL ~5% of the AZ's volumes into the stuck state.
AWS began disabling all communication between the degraded EBS cluster and the EBS control plane, quarantining the failure so it could no longer poison other zones.

A change to the EBS control plane fixed the elevated errors/latencies when launching EBS-backed EC2 instances in the healthy zones; new-instance error rates declined rapidly and returned to near-normal by Noon PDT.
The event was contained to the single affected AZ: stabilization complete, ~13% of the AZ's volumes still stuck, and EBS APIs disabled in the affected zone while recovery proceeded.

Installation of new physical storage capacity began. Recovery was slow because the EBS cluster will not reuse a failed node until every replica on it is successfully re-mirrored, and capacity had to be physically relocated from across the US East Region.
All but about 2.2% of the volumes in the affected AZ had been restored to normal operation.
EBS control-plane API access was re-enabled (finished enabling access) for the affected AZ.
Full EBS API access to EBS resources was restored to the affected Availability Zone.
All but 1.04% of the affected volumes had been recovered, largely by restoring from snapshots.
Manual recovery began on the remaining volumes that had not been snapshotted / were tied to hardware failures.

Remaining RDS databases were brought back online over the weekend, effectively ending the multi-day disruption; a final 0.07% of the affected AZ's EBS volumes could not be recovered. AWS's post-mortem describes RDS recovery as completing 'throughout the weekend' without a precise time; third-party summaries cite ~7:30 PM PDT Apr 24.

rootCause:
Immediate mechanism: At 12:47 AM PDT on 21 April 2011, AWS engineers ran a planned capacity upgrade on the primary EBS network in one US-East-1 Availability Zone. The procedure required shifting traffic off one router in the primary (high-capacity) EBS network onto another router in that same primary network. Instead, the change was executed so that traffic was routed onto the LOWER-CAPACITY redundant EBS network. That secondary network was never sized to carry primary load, so it too saturated/failed — and because the shift removed the primary path at the same moment, a large group of EBS storage nodes lost BOTH their primary and secondary network connectivity simultaneously. EBS nodes depend on continuous peer-to-peer connectivity to keep each volume's two replicas in sync; losing all connectivity made them believe their replicas had failed.

The specific failure that turned a network blip into a four-day outage was the EBS re-mirroring design. When connectivity was restored, every isolated node concurrently and aggressively began scanning the cluster for free space to rebuild a fresh second replica. Because so many volumes re-mirrored at once, the cluster's free capacity was exhausted almost instantly, and nodes that could not find space fell into a tight retry loop — the "re-mirroring storm". Roughly 13% of the AZ's volumes ended up "stuck", unable to serve I/O while hunting for storage. The storm then attacked a second, shared component: the region-wide EBS control plane. The torrent of Create Volume and re-mirror negotiation calls caused thread starvation in the control plane, and because that control plane is a single regional service, its degradation leaked EC2 launch/attach errors and elevated latencies into ALL Availability Zones — converting a single-AZ hardware event into a regional one. A latent, low-probability race condition (nodes failing while concurrently closing large batches of replication requests) added a second wave of ~5% more stuck volumes.

Latent / organisational root causes: (1) A change-management gap — a manual, error-prone network migration step with no automated guardrail to detect or block routing production EBS traffic onto a network known to lack the required capacity; the safeguard that should have caught it (capacity-aware validation or a peer-review/dry-run of the traffic-shift target) was absent or bypassed. (2) A design flaw in re-mirroring: it had no back-pressure, jitter, or admission control, so a correlated failure produced a stampede that consumed the very spare capacity meant to absorb failures — a classic positive-feedback loop. (3) A blast-radius / isolation flaw: the EBS control plane was a shared, region-scoped dependency with no per-AZ fault isolation, so one AZ's storm starved the whole region. (4) A hidden defect in the multi-AZ RDS failover path (a "previously un-encountered bug") meant 2.5% of the very databases customers had paid extra to make resilient did not fail over automatically.
contributingFactors: The redundant EBS network was lower-capacity than the primary and unable to sustain primary traffic, so routing to it was equivalent to removing redundancy rather than preserving it.
Re-mirroring had no rate-limiting, jitter, or back-pressure, allowing large numbers of nodes to stampede for free space simultaneously and exhaust cluster capacity.
The EBS control plane was a single region-wide service with no AZ-level isolation, so control-plane thread starvation propagated to healthy Availability Zones.
A latent, low-probability race condition caused EBS nodes to fail when concurrently closing large numbers of replication requests, generating a damaging second wave of stuck volumes.
A previously un-encountered bug in RDS multi-AZ failover prevented automatic failover for 2.5% of multi-AZ instances, undermining the paid resilience feature.
Recovery was structurally slow: a failed node cannot be reused until every replica on it is re-mirrored, and fresh capacity had to be physically relocated from elsewhere in the US East Region.

Slow, vague customer communications (imprecise 'small percentage'/'multiple availability zones' wording; AWS itself later conceded it wanted communications 'more frequent and containing more information') left customers unable to make informed failover decisions.
Many customers had architected for a single AZ, so a single-AZ event took their whole application down.

coe.action: Audit and automate the network change-management process so production EBS traffic can never be shifted onto an under-capacity network; add capacity-aware validation and reviewed dry-runs before executing traffic shifts.

Add back-pressure, rate-limiting and randomized retry (jitter) to EBS re-mirroring so a correlated failure cannot trigger a capacity-exhausting stampede, and make nodes more conservative about declaring a replica failed on transient network loss.
Improve EBS control-plane fault isolation so per-AZ failures cannot starve the region-wide control plane's threads/resources; reduce the shared, region-scoped blast radius.
Fix the previously un-encountered RDS multi-AZ failover bug so paid multi-AZ databases reliably auto-failover on stuck I/O.
Improve customer communications during large-scale events: more frequent, more specific status updates with actionable detail and clearer identification of affected AZs.
Provide better guidance and tooling for multi-AZ architecture so customers can build applications resilient to a single-AZ failure; issue the 10-day 100% service credit to affected customers.

lessonsLearnt: A recovery mechanism (re-mirroring) without admission control can become the outage: a correlated fault turns self-healing into a stampede that consumes the spare capacity meant to absorb failures.
Shared, region-scoped control planes are a hidden single point of failure — a per-AZ data-plane fault leaked region-wide because the control plane had no AZ isolation.
'Redundant' capacity that is lower-capacity than primary is not redundancy for full load; failing onto it can remove protection rather than preserve it.
Paid resilience features must be tested against the exact rare failure modes they exist for — the RDS multi-AZ failover bug surfaced only under real stress.
Single-AZ architectures inherit the AZ's fate; customers who spanned AZs and had snapshots recovered far better.
During large incidents, vague/slow status communications actively harm customers who could otherwise trigger their own failover.
improvements: Automated, capacity-aware guardrails in the network change process that block shifting production traffic onto an under-capacity path, plus mandatory peer-review/dry-run of the traffic-shift target.
Back-pressure, jitter and admission control in EBS re-mirroring to prevent stampedes.
Per-AZ isolation of the EBS control plane to bound blast radius.
Regression coverage and chaos/failure testing for the RDS multi-AZ failover path.
More frequent, more specific incident communications with clear affected-AZ identification.
Customer-facing multi-AZ architecture guidance and tooling to reduce single-AZ dependency.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Canonical control-plane cascade
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: a localized data-plane network misconfiguration in one AZ propagated region-wide because the EBS control plane was a single shared regional service subject to thread starvation.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Positive-feedback re-mirroring loop
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: reconnected nodes all re-mirrored at once, exhausting the free space that re-mirroring itself needed, so the more the system tried to heal the worse it got.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Two stacked amplifiers
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: (a) the re-mirroring stampede (~13%) and (b) a low-probability race condition on concurrent replication-request closure (~5%).

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Blast-radius containment held
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Blast-radius containment worked once AWS quarantined the degraded cluster from the control plane (08:20 PDT) and blocked Create Volume (02:40 PDT), restoring healthy AZs while the affected AZ was worked through the weekend.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Data durability held
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: only 0.07% of the affected AZ's volumes were permanently lost, and most recovery came from customer/EBS snapshots — reinforcing the snapshot discipline lesson.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: RDS single-AZ dependency exposed
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The RDS impact showed that a dependency on EBS turns an EBS event into a database event, and that the multi-AZ failover safeguard itself had an untested failure mode (2.5% did not fail over).

technicalDeepDive: EBS stores each volume as two replicas on separate storage nodes kept in sync over a peer-to-peer network. Normal operation uses a high-capacity primary network with a lower-capacity redundant network intended only for inter-node control/backup traffic. At 12:47 AM PDT on Apr 21, a capacity-upgrade step meant to move traffic between two routers on the primary network instead routed a large volume of traffic onto the low-capacity redundant network. That network saturated, and because the primary path had been withdrawn simultaneously, a large set of nodes lost all connectivity to their replica peers. Each node, unable to reach its replica, concluded the replica had failed and — upon reconnection — tried to establish a new replica by scanning the cluster for free space. With a large fraction of the cluster doing this at once, free capacity was consumed almost immediately; nodes that could not find space entered a continuous retry loop, leaving ~13% of the AZ's volumes 'stuck' (unable to serve I/O). The re-mirror negotiation and a flood of Create Volume calls then exhausted worker threads in the region-wide EBS control plane, so elevated latency/errors appeared across all AZs. AWS disabled Create Volume in the affected AZ (02:40), which recovered other AZs' EBS APIs by 02:50; but a low-probability race condition — nodes failing while concurrently closing large numbers of replication requests — drove a second wave (~5% more stuck) between 05:30 and 08:20, prompting AWS to sever the degraded cluster from the control plane (08:20). A control-plane fix at 11:30 restored EBS-backed EC2 launches to near-normal by noon; the event was contained to the single AZ by 12:04 PM. Recovery was slow because a failed node cannot be reused until all its replicas are re-mirrored and physical capacity had to be relocated across the region: 2.2% still down by Apr 22 12:30, 1.04% by Apr 24 12:30, with 0.07% permanently lost. RDS, which is layered on EBS, saw a peak 45% of single-AZ instances with stuck I/O (0.4% unrecoverable) and 2.5% of multi-AZ instances failing to auto-failover due to a previously un-encountered bug; RDS recovered over the following weekend.

references.title: Amazon EC2 cloud outage downs Reddit, Quora

references.title: Amazon EC2 Outage Brings Down Numerous Websites
references.quote: The outages began Thursday morning just before 5 a.m. ET; affected sites included Reddit, HootSuite, Foursquare, Quora, Heroku and Engine Yard.

fmea.scope: Amazon EBS in one US-East-1 Availability Zone and the region-wide EBS control plane: the network traffic-shift procedure used during a capacity upgrade, the primary and redundant EBS networks, the re-mirroring logic, the control plane's shared worker threads, the node-failure race condition, the recovery and capacity-replacement path, the RDS multi-AZ failover path layered on EBS, and customer communication. Analysed retrospectively from the official AWS post-mortem and the press record held in this dossier. Every AWS corrective action in the dossier is recorded as 'committed in post-mortem', so each revised score is a claim about the action, not a confirmed outcome.

modes.item: Network traffic-shift step in the capacity upgrade
modes.function: Move EBS traffic off one primary-network router onto another router in the same high-capacity primary network
modes.failureMode: Traffic is shifted onto the lower-capacity redundant EBS network instead, which saturates while the primary path is withdrawn
modes.effect: A large group of EBS nodes loses both primary and secondary connectivity at once, starting the re-mirroring storm that leads to about 90 hours of disruption
modes.cause: A manual, error-prone migration step with no automated check that the target network could carry the load
modes.prevention: None recorded beyond the planned procedure
modes.detection: None before execution; the shift was rolled back within minutes, after the nodes were already isolated

rationale.S: The chain it started degraded EBS, EC2 and RDS across the region for days and permanently lost 0.07% of the zone's volumes: the rubric's 9. Not 10: one zone hard down, no hazard to people.
rationale.O: A planned network upgrade is routine work, and choosing the wrong target in a manual step is a foreseeable slip that nothing guarded: 'occasional, weakly guarded'.
rationale.D: Nothing checked the target's capacity before the shift; AWS saw and rolled back the change only after the nodes had lost connectivity.

evidence.quote: the traffic was routed onto the lower capacity redundant EBS network
a manual, error-prone network migration step with no automated guardrail

actions.text: Audit and automate network change management, with capacity-aware validation and reviewed dry-runs before any traffic shift

modes.revisedRationale: Capacity-aware validation would flag an under-capacity target before execution (D 8→4) and a reviewed dry-run makes picking the wrong target less likely (O 6→3). The post-mortem records this as committed; the dossier does not record it as completed, so the reduction is a claim about the action, not a confirmed outcome. Severity is unchanged.

playbook.do: Check the target router and network capacity in a reviewed dry run before executing the traffic shift
Build capacity-aware validation into the shift tool so it refuses a target network that cannot carry the load
Alarm on EBS nodes losing both primary and secondary paths at once during a planned change
Roll the shift back as soon as nodes isolate, and pause the rest of the upgrade
Declare the incident, freeze further network changes in the region and tell the team the re-mirror storm is likely
Check which EBS nodes are still stuck after the rollback and track them to restore

modes.function: Carry EBS traffic when the primary path is unavailable
modes.failureMode: Sized only for inter-node control and backup traffic, so it cannot sustain primary load and fails when traffic lands on it
modes.effect: Routing onto the redundant path removes redundancy instead of preserving it; nodes lose both paths simultaneously
modes.cause: Design decision to build the redundant network at lower capacity than the primary
modes.detection: Seen at onset through node isolation

rationale.S: It is the reason the traffic-shift error became a loss of all connectivity rather than a slowdown, so it shares FM-01's severity.
rationale.O: A standing design condition that matters only when primary traffic is sent to it, an unusual event; kept below FM-01 so the same event is not counted twice at full weight.
rationale.D: The saturation was found by its effect on the nodes, after impact.

evidence.quote: a lower-capacity redundant network intended only for inter-node control/backup traffic

playbook.do: Size the redundant EBS network, or document that it cannot carry primary load, and make every runbook say so
Treat failover onto a lower-capacity path as a loss of redundancy in the change risk assessment
Alarm when traffic on the redundant EBS network passes its capacity
Move traffic back to the primary network as soon as the secondary saturates
Re-establish both paths to the isolated nodes and confirm connectivity to their replica peers

modes.function: Re-establish a lost replica without consuming the spare capacity meant to absorb failures
modes.failureMode: Every reconnected node searches for free space at once with no back-pressure or jitter, exhausting cluster capacity and looping on retries
modes.effect: About 13% of the zone's volumes become stuck and cannot serve I/O
modes.cause: No rate limiting, jitter, back-pressure or admission control in re-mirroring; nodes treat transient network loss as replica failure
modes.detection: Seen at onset as capacity exhaustion and stuck volumes

rationale.S: The dossier calls this the failure that turned a network blip into a four-day outage; it feeds the region-wide control-plane impact in FM-04.
rationale.O: Any correlated loss of connectivity triggers it, which is more than an unusual combination but not routine work.
rationale.D: The storm was visible as it began, but nothing in the design throttled it: 'detected at onset, not prevented'.

actions.text: Add back-pressure, rate limiting and jittered retry to re-mirroring, and make nodes more conservative about declaring a replica failed

modes.revisedRationale: Throttled, jittered re-mirroring should stop a correlated failure from becoming a capacity-exhausting stampede (O 5→2). Recorded as committed in the post-mortem, so this is a claim about the action, not a confirmed outcome. S and D unchanged.

playbook.do: Add back-pressure, jitter and admission control to re-mirroring so many nodes do not seek free space at once
Make nodes slower to declare a replica failed on a transient network loss
Alarm on cluster free capacity falling fast and on nodes entering a space-search retry loop
Throttle re-mirroring in the affected cluster by hand until free capacity stops falling
Ask for spare storage to be moved to the affected AZ before the cluster runs dry
Clear stuck volumes as capacity returns, oldest first, and report the count at every update

modes.function: Serve EBS API calls for every zone in the region without one zone's load affecting the others
modes.failureMode: A flood of Create Volume and re-mirror negotiation calls from one zone starves the shared control plane's threads
modes.effect: Elevated EBS error rates and latency in all zones; EBS-backed EC2 launches and attaches fail region-wide until Create Volume is disabled at 02:40 and the control-plane fix at 11:30
modes.cause: A single region-scoped control plane with no per-zone fault isolation
modes.detection: Internal monitoring after impact; consumer sites were already down by about 02:00 PDT

rationale.S: This is the step that made a single-zone event regional, across EBS, EC2 and RDS.
rationale.O: Needs a storm of the FM-03 kind in one zone first, which is infrequent.
rationale.D: AWS throttled Create Volume about 85 minutes after the starvation began, by which time public sites were already affected: detection after impact.

evidence.quote: converting a single-AZ hardware event into a regional one

actions.text: Improve control-plane fault isolation so one zone's failure cannot starve the region-wide control plane

modes.revisedRationale: With per-zone isolation the same storm would stay inside one zone (S 9→6). It does not make the storm less likely or easier to detect. Committed in the post-mortem; the reduction is a claim about the action, not a confirmed outcome.

playbook.do: Isolate the EBS control plane per AZ so one zone's load cannot starve the region
Alarm on control-plane thread pool use and on EBS API errors in healthy AZs, not only in the failed one
Disable Create Volume in the affected AZ to free control-plane threads, as done at 02:40
Sever the degraded cluster's link to the control plane to stop it poisoning other zones
Verify EBS-backed EC2 launches and attaches in the healthy AZs before the fix is called complete
Keep the affected AZ's EBS APIs disabled until the control plane is stable, then re-enable by zone

modes.function: Close large numbers of replication requests concurrently without the node failing
modes.failureMode: A latent, low-probability race condition makes nodes fail when closing many replication requests at once
modes.effect: A second wave between 05:30 and 08:20 PDT pushes about 5% more of the zone's volumes into the stuck state; AWS severs the degraded cluster from the control plane
modes.cause: Latent race condition exercised only under the storm's load
modes.detection: Internal monitoring after the second wave began

rationale.S: Adds stuck volumes inside the already-affected zone, after the healthy zones' APIs had recovered at 02:50: 'partial outage confined to one zone'.
rationale.O: Described as low-probability and needing an unusual load, so between 'remote' and 'infrequent'.
rationale.D: Found through the additional stuck volumes, after impact.

playbook.do: Add failure testing that closes large numbers of replication requests concurrently on one node
Alarm on EBS node crashes that cluster in time with replication request closes
Quarantine the degraded cluster from the control plane when a second wave of stuck volumes starts
Warn customers that a second wave is under way, and which volumes are likely hit
Patch the race condition on nodes in the cluster before they are returned to service

modes.function: Return stuck volumes to service and replace exhausted capacity quickly
modes.failureMode: Recovery runs for days because failed nodes cannot be reused until every replica on them is re-mirrored and new capacity must be physically relocated
modes.effect: 2.2% of volumes still down after about 36 hours, 1.04% after about 84 hours; RDS recovery runs into the weekend; 0.07% of the zone's volumes are never recovered
modes.cause: Node-reuse rule plus no spare capacity in place to absorb a cluster-wide exhaustion
modes.detection: None before the incident; the recovery time was learned during it

rationale.S: Sets the duration of a single-zone outage of a major service rather than its start; scored 8 rather than 9 because the healthy zones were restored by noon on the first day and the permanent loss was 0.07% of one zone's volumes.
rationale.O: Whenever a cluster's spare capacity is exhausted, recovery will run this slowly; the condition was present throughout.
rationale.D: No recorded exercise that would have revealed the recovery time before it mattered.

evidence.quote: a failed node cannot be reused until all its replicas are re-mirrored

playbook.do: Hold spare EBS capacity in each AZ so cluster-wide exhaustion has somewhere to go
Report free capacity and stuck volume count at every update so recovery time is estimated early
Install new physical storage in the affected AZ, drawn from across the US East Region
Restore volumes from snapshots wherever they exist, to bring them back faster than re-mirroring
Run manual recovery on volumes with no snapshot or tied to hardware failures
Keep EBS snapshots current and be ready to restore from them in another AZ

modes.function: Fail a paid multi-AZ database over automatically when its primary storage stalls
modes.failureMode: A previously un-encountered bug stops automatic failover for some multi-AZ instances
modes.effect: 2.5% of multi-AZ instances do not fail over; customers who paid for resilience stay down with the single-AZ fleet
modes.cause: Untested defect in the failover path
modes.detection: Customer-visible: databases that should have failed over did not

rationale.S: Major degradation of a major service for a subset of instances, and it defeats the feature meant to bound the impact.
rationale.O: Needs a stuck-I/O event of this scale to exercise the bug, which is infrequent.
rationale.D: No test had exercised the path; the bug showed itself only as failovers that did not happen.

actions.text: Fix the RDS multi-AZ failover bug
Add regression coverage and failure testing for the multi-AZ failover path

modes.revisedRationale: Fixing the known bug lowers the chance of this failure (O 3→2), and failure testing of the path would expose a similar defect before an incident (D 9→6). The fix is recorded as committed and the testing is listed as an improvement with no status, so both reductions are claims about the actions, not confirmed outcomes.

playbook.do: Add regression and chaos tests of the RDS multi-AZ failover path under stuck I/O
Check multi-AZ RDS instances against stuck I/O and alarm when one does not fail over on its own
Fail over the stalled multi-AZ instances by hand
Bring the remaining RDS databases online over the weekend, in order of customer impact
Restore your database from a snapshot or replica in another AZ if failover has not occurred

modes.function: Give customers frequent, specific status so they can decide whether to fail over
modes.failureMode: Updates are slow and vague about which zones and how much is affected
modes.effect: Customers cannot make informed failover decisions during a multi-day event
modes.cause: Not stated beyond AWS's own acknowledgement that it wanted communications more frequent and informative

rationale.S: It fails the communication, not the service, so 'customer-visible degradation'.
rationale.O: Present for any large event handled the same way: 'occasional'.
rationale.D: Recognised through customer reaction and AWS's later concession.

evidence.quote: We would like our communications to be more frequent and contain more information

actions.text: More frequent, more specific status updates with clear identification of affected zones

modes.revisedRationale: A defined standard for update frequency and detail makes vague updates less likely (O 6→3). Committed in the post-mortem; a claim about the action, not a confirmed outcome.

playbook.do: Set an update cadence and a template naming the affected AZs and the share of volumes hit
Compare status wording with the live stuck-volume count, and flag any update that understates the impact
Publish AZ-specific updates that say which APIs are disabled and which are healthy
Name a communications owner at the start of the incident and approve each update
Use the specific status to decide on failing over to another AZ without waiting for AWS

restored.quote: 2011-04-22 12:30 PDT All but about 2.2% of the volumes

durationBasis: Volumes stuck 00:47 PDT 21 Apr → all but 2.2% of affected-AZ volumes restored 12:30 PDT 22 Apr (35h43m)

roles.incident-commander: No incident commander is named in the record

roles.service-recovery: AWS EBS and RDS recovery engineers — not individually named
roles.comms: AWS Support and status-page communications — not in this sequence of events
roles.customer: EC2 customers such as Reddit, Quora, Foursquare, Hootsuite and Heroku

recorded.quote: engineers shifted traffic off a primary EBS router
recorded.did: Shift traffic during the capacity upgrade onto the lower-capacity redundant EBS network instead of a primary router

recorded.quote: The incorrect traffic shift was rolled back
recorded.did: Roll back the shift about three minutes later; the re-mirroring storm has already begun

recorded.quote: AWS disabled all Create Volume API requests in the affected AZ
recorded.did: Disable Create Volume in the affected AZ at 02:40 to relieve control-plane thread starvation

recorded.quote: AWS began disabling all communication between the degraded EBS cluster and the EBS control plane
recorded.did: Cut the degraded cluster off from the control plane at 08:20 to stop it poisoning other zones

recorded.quote: Installation of new physical storage capacity began.
recorded.did: Begin installing new storage capacity on 22 April, relocated from across the US East Region

recorded.quote: Manual recovery began on the remaining volumes
recorded.did: Manually recover volumes with no snapshot or tied to hardware failures
